Solder preform feeding · converts generic tin wire into precise chips at the mounter

Your stencil handles the small pads. Who handles the big ones?
One tin wire. Eight chip sizes. Any mounter. 36 mm wide.

The SSPC101 is a solder tin chip feeder that converts standard no-flux tin wire into precise preformed solder chips on-demand, at the pick-and-place machine. A stepper motor drives a precision cam mechanism that presses and forms the wire; an air cylinder cuts each chip to length; the mounter nozzle picks the finished preform and places it on the pad that needs extra solder volume. Eight chip sizes from 0402 to 1510, ±0.5 mm accuracy, 0.1 seconds per piece at peak speed — in a body only 36 mm wide and 3.5 kg light.

01 — Why it matters

One stencil thickness cannot solder a 0201 resistor and a 12 mm connector on the same board

Miniaturisation pushed component sizes down, but connectors, transformers, battery holders and power inductors stayed large. The same PCB now carries 0.5 mm pitch fine-pitch parts next to through-hole-adjacent pads that need three times the solder volume. A single stencil thickness serves one of those worlds — and the other one gets voids, cold joints, or a hand-soldering rework bench. The SSPC101 puts the extra solder exactly where the stencil cannot, using the mounter you already own.

01

The stencil compromise

Solder paste volume is set by stencil thickness × aperture area. A thin stencil for 0201 passives starves a 12 mm power pad. A thick stencil for the power pad bridges the 0201. You choose which defect to accept — or you add solder locally.

02

Existing fixes cost more than the problem

Manual paste dispensing adds labour and inconsistency. Stepped stencils cost 3–5× a normal stencil and wear fast under the squeegee. Commercial preformed tin reels carry high unit prices, MOQ commitments, and flux-free chips that still need a separate flux application.

03

The mounter is already there

Every SMT line has a pick-and-place machine with idle nozzles between component picks. The SSPC101 feeds solder chips into that same nozzle path — no second machine, no extra conveyor, no new operator station. The mounter places solder the same way it places a resistor.

02 — The method

From tin wire spool to placed preform in six repeatable moves

The SSPC101 turns a commodity — 1 kg of generic no-flux tin wire on a plastic spool — into up to 421,000 precisely sized solder preforms (0402 size), each one placed by your existing mounter nozzle. The document calls it '锡丝压制、成形' — press and form the wire. Here is the full sequence.

01

Load the wire

A standard spool of no-flux tin wire mounts on the reel holder at the rear of the feeder. The wire diameter sets the chip size: 0.5 mm for 0402, 2.0 mm for 1510. Any brand of wire works — the document notes that different alloys produce slightly different formed dimensions.

02

Feed and press

A stepper motor drives the wire forward through a precision cam mechanism. The cam presses the round wire flat to the target thickness — 0.3 mm for 0402 up to 1.3 mm for 1510. Pure electric, no hydraulic variation, no warm-up drift.

03

Cut to length

An air cylinder drives the cutting blade across the flattened wire at the programmed length. The cut is clean and repeatable: ±0.5 mm feeding accuracy means every chip is the same size the mounter's vision system expects.

04

Present to the nozzle

The finished chip sits at the pick position, in a known attitude and at a known height. The mounter nozzle descends, vacuums the chip, and lifts it — the same motion it performs ten thousand times per shift for resistors and capacitors.

05

Place on the pad

The mounter places the solder chip on the pad that needs extra volume — typically alongside or on top of the stencil-printed paste. During reflow, the preform melts and fuses with the paste, giving the joint its full solder fill without a second process step.

Process sequence and chip specifications are quoted from the Solder Preform Feeder introduction document (20220304) and the specification sheet.

Built around one idea: solder volume is a placement problem, not a printing problem

Precision cam mechanism, pure electric

The document's own words: '纯电动，精密凸轮组，出料速度达0.1秒/粒'. No hydraulics, no warm-up drift, no air-pressure variation in the forming step. The stepper motor and cam define the chip geometry; the air cylinder only cuts.

36 mm wide — fits the slot you already have

The feeder body is 500 × 36 × 100 mm and weighs 3.5 kg. It occupies one standard tape-feeder slot on the mounter bank. No extra rail, no second table, no floor space that you do not already have.

Any wire, any brand

The document specifies: '可对应任意品牌锡丝（不含助焊剂锡丝，减少助焊剂飞溅）'. No-flux wire from any supplier works — and no-flux means no spatter in the reflow oven, no residue under the component, no cleaning step.

Works with paste, not against it

'与锡膏搭配使用，提高焊点锡量，增强焊点强度' — the preform supplements the stencil-printed paste on pads that need extra volume. The joint gets its solder fill from both sources; neither process is compromised.

Eight sizes on one feeder

From 0402 (1.0 × 0.7 × 0.3 mm) to 1510 (4.0 × 2.5 × 1.3 mm). Change the wire and the accessory set, and the same feeder body produces the next size. No second machine for the next product.

One motor, one cylinder, one connector — controls an operator actually uses

Stepper motor drive

The feed and form step is a stepper motor at up to 600 rpm. Digital, repeatable, no mechanical wear adjustment. The motor speed sets the chip pitch; the cam profile sets the chip thickness.

Air cylinder cutter

The cut is pneumatic — 0.4–0.6 MPa drives the blade across the formed wire. Simple, fast, and the blade is the only consumable. The document notes: different wire alloys produce slightly different formed dimensions; the cut length compensates.

8-core connector

Power, ground and the IO handshake arrive through one 8-core φ16 mm connector — the same interface standard used across the Southern Machinery feeder family. Plug in, and the mounter knows the feeder is there.

Material sensor

The low-material detection is continuous: three consecutive misses and the feeder alarms. No optical alignment ritual, no sensitivity dial. The sensor watches the pick position; if the chip is not there, the line knows.

06 — Installation

Five moves from spool to first placed chip

The product document defines the whole commissioning: mechanical install, wire loading, size configuration, IO handshake, and the first-placement verification. Plan for minutes, not hours.

STEP 1 · Unbox and inspect

Check the body, reel holder, cam mechanism, cutting cylinder, material sensor and 8-core connector against the parts list. Confirm the wire path is clean and the blade is sharp.

STEP 2 · Mount on the bank

Slide the 36 mm body into a standard tape-feeder slot. The connector mates with the bank supply. No tools, no shims — the same slot geometry that holds your tape feeders.

STEP 3 · Load the wire

Mount the spool on the rear holder and thread the wire through the guide, under the cam, past the blade. The wire diameter must match the chip size you selected.

STEP 4 · Connect and configure

Plug the 8-core connector. Set the chip size on the mounter's feeder data. The stepper motor indexes; the air cylinder cuts; the sensor verifies the first three chips.

STEP 5 · Verify the first placement

Run a test placement onto a scrap board. Check the chip position under the mounter vision. Measure the formed dimensions against the spec table. Log the result — your next changeover starts from a known setting.

ARTICLE 01The 0201-and-a-connector problem: why your stencil is a compromise

One board, two solder-volume worlds. The maths of why a single thickness cannot serve both, and the three existing fixes that cost more than the defect.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the Solder Preform Feeder product document and specification sheet.

Open a modern PCB assembly drawing and count the component sizes. A 0201 resistor sits 0.4 mm from a 12 mm power connector. The resistor needs 0.05 mg of solder; the connector needs 15 mg. Your stencil has one thickness.

This is the compromise every SMT engineer knows but rarely names: the stencil is designed for the majority, and the minority gets defects. A thin stencil for fine-pitch passives starves the power pad — cold joint, insufficient fillet, a thermal cycle that cracks the connection in the field. A thick stencil for the power pad bridges the 0201 — solder ball, short, a rework ticket. The stepped stencil solves the problem by changing thickness locally, but costs 3–5× a normal stencil, wears under the squeegee, and still limits how much extra volume you can add.

Here is the five-minute audit. Pull your three highest-defect board types. For each, identify the pads that failed reflow inspection for insufficient solder or bridging. Count them. Multiply by your monthly volume. Then ask: how many rework minutes did those pads cost last quarter? The answer is your preform budget.

The SSPC101 addresses the problem at the only point where it can be solved without changing the stencil: the placement step. A 36 mm-wide feeder in a standard tape slot converts cheap no-flux tin wire into precisely sized solder chips — eight sizes from 0402 to 1510 — and presents them to the mounter nozzle. The chip lands on the pad that needs extra volume, alongside the stencil-printed paste. During reflow, both melt together. The joint gets its full fill; the stencil stays thin; the 0201 stays clean.

The compounding part: once solder volume is a placement variable, not a printing variable, your process design changes. New products with new pad geometries stop requiring new stencils. The preform is a component in your BOM, placed by the same machine, programmed in the same file. The rework bench shrinks by the number of pads you audited.

Run the five-minute audit this week. Then send us the three board types, the pad geometry and the defect count — info@smthelp.com or WhatsApp +86 13602562576 — and we will tell you which chip size fits, how much wire you will consume, and what the payback looks like on your numbers.

ARTICLE 02What 421,000 chips per kilogram tells you about solder cost

The yield table that changes the preform conversation from 'how much per piece' to 'how much per joint' — and why generic wire wins.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the Solder Preform Feeder product document and specification sheet.

The specification sheet for the SSPC101 contains a number that changes the preform conversation entirely: 421,000 chips per kilogram of wire. Not per reel. Not per pack. Per kilogram of generic, commodity tin wire.

Commercial preformed solder chips are sold by the piece, with MOQ commitments that make small runs expensive and large runs political. The unit price includes the forming service, the packaging, the inventory risk and the margin on a specialised product. You are paying for geometry that your own feeder can create in 0.1 seconds.

The method is simple arithmetic. Take your monthly chip consumption for the pads that need extra solder. Divide by 421,000 (for 0402) or 7,200 (for 1510). That is your wire consumption in kilograms. Multiply by your wire price per kilogram — a commodity figure you already know from your soldering station budget. The result is your solder cost per joint, and it is almost certainly lower than the preform reel price.

The SSPC101 makes this arithmetic real because it converts the wire at the machine, on demand, in the size you need today. Eight standard sizes on one feeder body; change the accessory, not the machine. The document notes: different alloys produce slightly different formed dimensions — the cam compensates. No MOQ, no lead time on specialised reels, no inventory of preforms for products you no longer build.

Track the wire consumption alongside your paste consumption. After a quarter, you will have a real cost-per-joint figure for solder volume, and the preform reel supplier's quotation will look like what it is: a premium for geometry you can make yourself.

Send us your monthly pad count and preferred alloy. We will calculate the wire consumption, recommend the chip size, and quote the feeder with the accessory set.

ARTICLE 030.1 seconds per chip: the cam mechanism that keeps ahead of the nozzle

Why pure-electric precision cam beats pneumatic forming on repeatability, and what 600 rpm actually means at the pick position.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the Solder Preform Feeder product document and specification sheet.

Every feeder on your bank has a speed. The number that matters is not the peak — it is the speed at which accuracy holds. The SSPC101's document publishes both: 1.2 seconds per piece standard, 0.1 seconds per piece peak, and ±0.5 mm feeding accuracy.

Consider what 0.1 seconds means mechanically. The stepper motor indexes at up to 600 rpm; the precision cam presses the wire flat; the air cylinder cuts. In one tenth of a second, a round wire becomes a rectangular chip with defined length, width and thickness. The cam profile sets the geometry; the motor speed sets the rate. No warm-up drift, no air-pressure variation in the forming step — the document specifies '纯电动，精密凸轮组' for exactly this reason.

The method for sizing your feeder to your line is to compare two numbers. Your mounter's placement cycle time — the interval between successive nozzle descents — is the demand. The feeder's output rate is the supply. At 0.1 s/piece peak, the SSPC101 keeps ahead of even a multi-nozzle head placing 0402 passives. At the 1.2 s standard pace, it covers the typical solder-chip placement rate on a mixed-technology board where preforms go on a handful of pads per board, not hundreds.

The accuracy figure — ±0.5 mm — is what makes the speed useful. A chip placed at the wrong position is a defect the same as a chip not placed at all. The stepper motor's digital indexing and the cam's mechanical repeatability hold the position within the mounter's vision tolerance, cycle after cycle. The three-miss alarm is the safety net: if the chip is not there, the line knows before the next board arrives.

Log the motor speed and the chip dimensions on your process card. The first time a new alloy or wire diameter arrives, you will know from the card what to set before you set it.

If your placement cycle demands faster than 0.1 s/piece, tell us the machine model and the nozzle count. We will size the cam profile for your rate.

ARTICLE 04No-flux wire, no spatter: the reflow-cleanliness argument nobody makes

The hidden cost of flux in preformed solder — oven contamination, cleaning cycles, residue under components — and why the document specifies no-flux.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the Solder Preform Feeder product document and specification sheet.

The reflow oven does not care where your solder came from. It cares about what is in it — and what is not. The SSPC101's document specifies no-flux wire for a reason that is visible in the oven's maintenance log, not the BOM.

Flux is necessary for wetting — it removes oxides and allows the solder to flow onto the pad. But flux in a preformed chip means flux in your reflow oven during every reflow cycle. It spatters. It deposits on the oven walls, the thermocouples, the conveyor rails. It leaves residue under the component body, which can interfere with conformal coating adhesion or create ionic contamination paths under voltage. Every cleaning cycle is a line stop; every residue defect is an escape.

The method the document encodes is separation of concerns: the stencil-printed paste carries the flux needed for wetting; the preform contributes the metal volume needed for the joint. The wire is no-flux — '不含助焊剂锡丝，减少助焊剂飞溅' — because the paste already provides the chemistry. The chip is pure metal, placed where the paste is thin, and it melts into the joint without adding a second flux system to the oven atmosphere.

This is why the document emphasises '与锡膏搭配使用' — used alongside solder paste. The preform does not replace the paste; it supplements the volume. The paste wets; the preform fills. The joint gets its fillet, its shear strength and its X-ray density without the oven paying a contamination tax.

Track your oven cleaning frequency before and after. The reduction in spatter-related maintenance is a saving the payback calculator does not count, but the maintenance log does.

Tell us your current alloy and paste system. We will confirm the no-flux wire compatibility and the formed chip dimensions for your reflow profile.

ARTICLE 0536 mm wide: why the feeder's footprint is the compatibility spec that matters

The bank slot is the real estate. What 'fits one standard tape slot' means for your line layout, and why 500 × 36 × 100 mm is a design decision, not a coincidence.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the Solder Preform Feeder product document and specification sheet.

The specification sheet lists the body as 500 × 36 × 100 mm. The number that matters is the 36.

Every mounter feeder bank is a real-estate market. Slots are allocated by tape width: 8 mm, 12 mm, 16 mm, 24 mm, 32 mm, 44 mm. A feeder that needs 56 mm takes two slots and a negotiation. A feeder that fits in 36 mm takes one slot — the same slot that holds your 0402 tape — and the conversation is over.

The SSPC101's 36 mm width is a design decision, not a coincidence. The document lists the body dimensions alongside the compatible mounter table for a reason: the feeder is engineered to occupy the same physical interface as the tape feeders already on your bank. No extra rail, no second table, no floor space that you do not already have. The 500 mm length runs parallel to the bank; the 100 mm height clears the nozzle path.

At 3.5 kg, one person installs it. Slide it in, plug the 8-core connector, load the wire spool. The mounter's feeder data screen recognises it. The total commissioning is a same-shift job, and the total footprint is one slot on a bank that already has forty.

Measure your bank. Count the slots. If you have one free slot and a pad that needs extra solder, the 36 mm width is the spec that makes the SSPC101 possible on your line without a layout change.

ARTICLE 06The three-miss alarm: stopping the line before the defect reaches AOI

Detection as a process design choice. Why 'three consecutive misses' is the right number, and what silent starvation costs a high-mix line.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the Solder Preform Feeder product document and specification sheet.

A silent starvation is the most expensive failure mode on a high-mix line, because the defect is not discovered where it is created.

The feeder runs out of wire. The nozzle descends onto an empty pick position. The mounter's vision system, depending on its configuration, either alarms (and the line stops, costing a cycle) or passes (and the board continues to reflow without its solder chip). The board reaches AOI. The AOI either catches the void (and the board goes to rework, costing a ticket) or does not (and the board ships, and the field return costs a reputation). The cost escalates by an order of magnitude at each stage.

The SSPC101's specification closes this gap at the source: three consecutive failed feeds trigger an alarm. Not a warning. Not a log entry. An alarm — the same signal class that stops the mounter for a mis-pick or a tape-end. The document's exact words: '连续3次缺料，送料异常报警'. Three is the right number because one miss can be a fluke (a slightly irregular chip, a momentary air-pressure dip); three in a row is a process condition, and a process condition deserves a line stop.

The method is to treat the feeder as a process step, not a peripheral. The sensor watches the pick position. The alarm is wired through the 8-core connector into the mounter's control system. The operator sees the same alarm class they see for every other feeder on the bank. There is no 'check the solder feeder later' — the line stops, the wire is replaced, and the board that would have been voided was never started.

Review your AOI escape rate for solder-volume defects. If any of them trace back to a feeder that ran dry, the three-miss alarm is the cheapest insurance you will ever buy.

Want the alarm wiring diagram? The 8-core connector pinout is in the product document, and our engineers will confirm the signal mapping for your mounter before installation.

ARTICLE 07Paste plus preform: the combined process that neither does alone

The document's core use case explained — why the preform supplements the stencil rather than replacing it, and how the joint gets its full fill.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the Solder Preform Feeder product document and specification sheet.

The document's most important sentence is not a specification. It is a process instruction: '与锡膏搭配使用，提高焊点锡量，增强焊点强度' — used alongside solder paste, increase the solder volume of the joint, strengthen the joint.

This is not a replacement story. The stencil still prints the paste. The paste still wets the pad and provides the flux chemistry. What the preform adds is metal volume at the specific pads where the stencil's single thickness cannot deliver enough. The chip lands on the paste-covered pad; during reflow, both melt; the joint gets its full fillet and shear strength without a second printing step or a thicker stencil that would bridge the neighbouring fine-pitch components.

The method for designing the combined process is to treat the preform as a BOM component. In the mounter program, the solder chip is placed like any other part — same nozzle, same vision, same feeder data. The pad geometry determines the chip size: a 12 mm connector pad that needs 15 mg of solder gets a 1510 preform on top of its stencil-printed paste. A 4 mm power pad that needs 3 mg gets a 1206. The stencil stays at the thickness your fine-pitch components need.

The combined process also solves the rework problem at its root. Cold joints and insufficient-fillet escapes that used to arrive at ICT or functional test are prevented at placement — because the solder volume is correct before the board enters the oven. The rework bench shrinks; the first-pass yield rises; the customer never sees the joint that would have failed.

Map your pads against the eight chip sizes. The ones that need more solder than your stencil delivers are your preform candidates. The ones that do not — leave them to the paste.

ARTICLE 08Before you buy solder preforms by the reel, run these four numbers

A payback method with your own volumes, your own defect rate and your own price — plus the four savings the method deliberately leaves out.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the Solder Preform Feeder product document and specification sheet.

Most payback conversations about soldering automation are dishonest in the same direction: the vendor's spreadsheet finds savings you will never collect. Here is the opposite method — four lines, your numbers, and a bias toward under-claiming.

Line one: what does the rework bench cost today? Count the pads per board that need extra solder, the boards per day, and the seconds per hand-rework joint you measured yourself — not the number from a brochure, your number. Line two: what does the feeder actually eliminate? Be honest: it prevents the voids and cold joints on the preform pads, not every defect on the board. Use the share your process really allows. Line three: your loaded wage and your working days. Line four: divide the quoted feeder price by the annual rework labour the first three lines freed. If the answer is under twelve months, this is a financial decision, not a capital debate.

The calculator on this page runs those four lines exactly, with nothing pre-baked. No invented defect rates, no competitor-bashing multipliers, no price hard-coded anywhere — every money figure is typed in by you.

Now the four savings the method deliberately leaves out, because they are yours to prove: the stepped-stencil premium you stop paying (3–5× per stencil, every revision); the commercial preform reel markup you avoid (MOQ, unit price, inventory of sizes you no longer need); the void escapes that never reach the customer (warranty, reputation, the field return that costs ten times the rework); and the oven cleaning cycles you skip because no-flux wire does not spatter.

Every factory that starts measuring solder-volume defects finds them hiding in someone else's cost line — usually 'rework' or 'warranty'. The four lines make them visible, and visible is negotiable.

Send us the four numbers. We will turn them into a chip-size recommendation, a wire consumption estimate, and a quotation that matches the arithmetic you already trust.

13 — FAQ

Answers to the questions this feeder raises

What solder chip sizes does the SSPC101 produce?
Eight standard sizes: 0402 (1.0 × 0.7 × 0.3 mm), 0603 (1.6 × 0.9 × 0.4 mm), 0603T (1.6 × 1.0 × 0.5 mm), 0805 (2.0 × 1.2 × 0.45 mm), 0805T (2.0 × 1.3 × 0.6 mm), 1206 (3.2 × 1.6 × 0.6 mm), 1206T (3.2 × 1.8 × 1.0 mm) and 1510 (4.0 × 2.5 × 1.3 mm). Each size uses a specific wire diameter from 0.5 to 2.0 mm. Custom chip geometries are available on request.
Does it fit any mounter other than the six listed brands?
The product document states: '可定制任一贴片机品牌与型号' — customisable for any pick-and-place brand and model. The six listed (YAMAHA, JUKI, PANASONIC, FUJI, SAMSUNG, ASM) are the documented standard interfaces. Tell us your machine and we quote the connector variant.
How fast can it feed? What throughput should I plan?
The published feeding speed is 1.2 s per piece standard, with the precision cam mechanism reaching 0.1 s per piece at peak. At 600 rpm motor speed, the feed keeps ahead of any mounter placement cycle. The document's own words: '纯电动，精密凸轮组，出料速度达0.1秒/粒'.
What happens when the wire runs out or a chip fails to form?
The material sensor monitors the pick position continuously. Three consecutive failed feeds trigger an alarm on the mounter — the line stops before the defect reaches AOI. The alarm is not a warning; it is a process interlock.
What are the power and utility requirements?
DC 24 V for the stepper motor and sensor, and 0.4 – 0.6 MPa dry clean compressed air for the cutting cylinder. Both arrive through the 8-core φ16 mm connector and the standard air line. No external supply, no software licence.
Do I need special tin wire, or will any spool work?
Any brand of no-flux tin wire works — the document specifies '可对应任意品牌锡丝（不含助焊剂锡丝）'. The wire diameter must match the chip size you selected. Different alloys (SAC305, Sn63Pb37, lead-free) produce slightly different formed dimensions; the spec table notes this.
How long does installation and chip-size changeover take?
Mounting is a slide-and-plug into a standard 36 mm tape-feeder slot — seconds, with no tools. A chip-size changeover is swapping the wire spool and the forming accessory. The full commissioning, including the first-placement verification, is a same-shift job.
How do I get a quotation?
Send your pad geometry (which pads need extra solder), your board volumes, your mounter model and your preferred alloy to info@smthelp.com or WhatsApp +86 13602562576. You get a chip-size recommendation, a wire consumption estimate, a spare part kit proposal and a price — usually within one working day.
